summaries.example: Imagine a map of a town. The map can show where roads go, but it may not answer why the town exists or why people built it. In a similar way, science can study how the universe changes, while theology asks questions about God and creation. The two kinds of questions can overlap, but one does not automatically settle the other.
summaries.summary: Cosmology studies the universe, while theology studies religious ideas about God and creation. The entry explains how these subjects have interacted, especially in discussions of the big bang. An expanding universe with a finite age may seem to fit the belief that God created the universe, but this conclusion is not simple. Some religious beliefs do not require a beginning in time, and some theists interpret creation as the universe depending on God at every moment. Also, the big bang models do not describe a first moment in the ordinary way, and general relativity may not work in the extreme conditions near the big bang. Future theories using quantum physics could change the picture. Steady-state, cyclic, multiverse, and other models show that cosmology has been linked with both religious and nonreligious ideas. The main lesson is that science and theology can raise related questions without one simple answer deciding the whole debate.
key_ideas: Scientific cosmology uses mathematics, observations, and testable predictions to study the universe.
Many religious thinkers connect the universe’s history with questions about God, but religious beliefs are diverse.
The big bang model suggests that the universe has a finite age, yet it does not by itself prove or disprove God’s existence.
Other ideas, such as steady-state, cyclic, quantum, and multiverse models, lead to different discussions about creation.
Scientists still do not know whether the big bang was the absolute beginning of everything.
summaries.why_it_matters: Questions about the universe can affect how people think about meaning, God, evidence, and the limits of science. Learning about several viewpoints helps us avoid saying that one scientific discovery automatically proves a religious belief or disproves it. It also shows why careful thinking is important when a scientific model is used to answer a philosophical question.

important_terms.definition: The study of the universe, including its size, history, contents, and possible future.
Thinking about God, religious beliefs, and questions about creation and existence.
The view that God exists and is connected with the universe.
The idea that God made the universe from nothing.
A scientific model in which the universe has been expanding from a very hot, dense early condition.
A point in a scientific model where the usual description of space and time breaks down.

questions_to_think_about: Can a scientific model answer every question about why anything exists?
Why might two people with different religious beliefs understand the same discovery differently?
Does having a beginning in a model necessarily mean that God caused it?
What evidence would help scientists compare different cosmological models?

summaries.example: Suppose a model says that a balloon’s surface has been expanding and that, when the equations are run backward, its size approaches zero at a limiting point. One person might say this supports a created universe. Another might note that the model contains no ordinary first state and that the theory may fail under the extreme conditions near that limit. The disagreement concerns both the physics and what “creation” means.
summaries.summary: Cosmology and theology address overlapping questions, but they do so by different methods and with different standards of explanation. Scientific cosmology builds mathematical models constrained by observation, while theology and metaphysics ask about creation, dependence, purpose, and the existence of anything at all. The big bang model and relativistic cosmology have sometimes been presented as evidence for creation because they describe a universe with a finite past. The entry cautions that this argument depends on a particular version of theism. Some theists regard creation as timeless dependence on God, and others hold religious views that conflict with the universe’s scientifically estimated age. Moreover, Friedmann-Robertson-Walker models have a singular boundary rather than a clearly represented first state. General relativity may also be unreliable near that boundary, where quantum effects should matter. Quantum, cyclic, steady-state, and multiverse models therefore complicate any simple link between cosmology and theism or atheism. The historical record likewise shows little stable connection between cosmologists’ religious commitments and the models they defend. The entry’s broad conclusion is not that science and theology never meet, but that their relationship requires careful distinctions about evidence, explanation, model limits, and the meaning of creation.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes scientific cosmology from philosophical and theological cosmologies while emphasizing their historical interaction.

The inference from a finite-age universe to theism is not straightforward: not all theists require a temporal beginning, and some interpretations of religion conflict with the scientific age of the universe.
A big bang singularity is a feature of a model, not automatically a physical event at which God created a first state.
General relativity is not tested in the extreme quantum-gravitational regime near a singularity, so classical results may not settle the universe’s ultimate beginning.
Steady-state and cyclic models show that an eternal universe can be interpreted as either a challenge to theism or as compatible with continual divine creation.
Multiverse and anthropic proposals are interpreted differently: some see them as alternatives to design explanations, while others argue that theism could accommodate them.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic is a useful case study in philosophy of science. It shows how an empirical theory can be extended into a metaphysical argument, and why that extension needs its own justification. It also illustrates underdetermination: different cosmological models and different theological interpretations may fit, reinterpret, or challenge one another in more than one way. Understanding these distinctions supports informed discussion without reducing either science or religion to a slogan.

important_terms.definition: The scientific study of the universe as a whole, using physical theories, mathematics, astronomical observations, and testable predictions.
The view that God exists and is the ultimate creator or sustainer of the universe; the entry stresses that theism has many forms.
The doctrine that the universe depends on God for its existence, traditionally sometimes understood as being made from nothing.
A family of relativistic models describing a large-scale homogeneous and isotropic universe whose expansion is represented by a scale factor.
A boundary or breakdown in a spacetime model, often associated with paths of finite length that cannot be extended farther.
Einstein’s theory in which spacetime responds dynamically to matter and energy through gravitational field equations.
A proposal that combines quantum theory with cosmology; some versions allow a pre-big-bang phase or remove the classical singularity.
The hypothesis that many universes or cosmic regions exist, often used to discuss why our universe has life-permitting conditions.

questions_to_think_about: What additional premise is needed to move from “the universe has a finite age” to “God created the universe”?
Should cosmology describe a miracle if a miracle occurred, or should it describe only laws that normally govern universes?
Does a model with no first spacetime state rule out a creator, or only a particular picture of creation?
How should evidence be weighed when a theory has strong explanatory appeal but limited testability?
Can the anthropic principle explain life-permitting conditions without deciding whether a designer exists?

summaries.example: A class studies a computer simulation of an expanding universe. When students run it backward, the program reaches a limit where its rules no longer work. One student says, “That proves someone started the universe.” Another says, “It shows only what this simulation can describe.” A third adds, “Some religious people think creation means dependence on God, not a first event in time.” The class has discovered why the same scientific result can support different philosophical conclusions.
summaries.summary: The entry examines the meeting point between scientific cosmology and theology, especially debates about God, creation, and the big bang. Scientific cosmology uses physics, mathematics, observations, and predictions. Theology considers religious claims about God and the universe. Because these fields ask related questions, people have sometimes argued that an expanding universe with a finite age confirms the idea that God created it. The entry explains why that argument needs caution. Different theists have different beliefs: some expect a young universe, some accept the scientific age, and some understand creation as the universe’s continuing dependence on God rather than as an event at a particular time. Also, the big bang is represented in some models by a singularity, where the model cannot describe an earlier state. That does not by itself establish a first physical moment or a divine cause. General relativity may fail in the very early universe, so quantum cosmology could change our understanding. Older and newer alternatives, including steady-state, cyclic, and multiverse theories, can be interpreted in religious or nonreligious ways. The entry therefore rejects a simple story in which one scientific model proves theism or another proves atheism.
key_ideas: Scientific cosmology and religious cosmology ask some of the same large questions, but they use different kinds of reasoning.
The big bang may seem to support creation because it describes a universe with a finite age, but this depends on what a person means by creation and which religious view is being considered.
Not all theists think God’s creation requires a first moment in time.
A scientific model’s singularity should not automatically be treated as a literal moment when the universe began or as proof of a creator.
General relativity may not give the final story near the big bang because quantum effects become important there.
Steady-state, cyclic, quantum, and multiverse theories show that science does not offer only one possible connection between cosmology and religion.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic matters because people often use scientific ideas to make claims about meaning and God. Studying the arguments teaches us to separate what a theory directly predicts from the larger philosophical conclusions someone draws from it. It also encourages respectful discussion: neither “science has settled every religious question” nor “religion can decide scientific models” captures the variety of views described in the entry.

important_terms.definition: The study of the universe as a whole: its beginning or past, structure, changes, and possible future.
The study of religious ideas about God, creation, and the universe.
Belief in God or gods; in this entry, the focus is mainly on western monotheistic traditions, especially varieties of Christianity.
The belief that God created the universe out of nothing, though some thinkers understand creation as continuing dependence on God.
A scientific picture in which the universe has expanded from an extremely hot and dense early condition.
A place where a scientific theory’s description reaches a limit, such as a model that cannot describe an earlier time.
A theory of gravity that treats space and time as changing together with matter and energy.
A family of ideas in which the universe may continue through repeated cycles rather than having one absolute beginning.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a scientific discovery support one person’s religious view but challenge another’s?
What is the difference between saying that God began the universe and saying that the universe depends on God at every moment?
Why should scientists be cautious about using a theory outside the conditions where it has been tested?
Could an eternal universe still be described as created? What would “created” mean in that case?
Does a theory that explains why a universe can exist also explain why there is anything at all?
